utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registrar call the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-95-4-PT, The Prosecutor versus Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic; case number IT-95-8-PT, The Prosecutor versus Zigic; case number IT-97-24-PT, The Prosecutor versus Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Brenda Hollis, and I along, with my colleagues, Michael Keegan and Ann Sutherland, appear on behalf of The Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. For the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dusan Vucicevic, together with Professor D'Amato, on behalf of Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: Defence counsel Tosic appear on behalf of the accused Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUBERINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, lawyer Veljko Guberina, Belgrade, appearing as Defence counsel for the accused Mladen Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am for the defence on Mr. Kvocka, replacement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your name, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Slavica Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, can the defendants all hear in a language which they understand? Can you hear? Very well. Now, these cases are being listed together for this reason: The case of Milan Kovacevic was due to be tried today, but the Prosecutor, as those in the case will know, applied to amend the indictment, and that motion was refused by the Trial Chamber. Against that decision the Prosecutor has appealed, and the Appeal Chamber hasss not yet decided the appeal. So the position is this, that the trial of Mr. Kovacevic cannot start today and, indeed, cannot start until the Appeals Chamber has determined the appeal. Meanwhile, the other three accused have appeared before another Trial Chamber, and the Prosecutor now applies for the joinder of these cases or, rather, the concurrent presentation of evidence, as it is put, and that motion is listed for hearing today together with a number of motions in the case of Milan Kovacevic. It is obviously convenient to hear the motion for joinder first, and that we will turn to now. Ms. Grahovac, I wonder if I could address you on behalf of the Defence counsel? The position is this, that the Defence in your cases have not yet, as we understood it, received any of the material; is that right? Is that right? Perhaps you could confirm it so we can have it on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUBERINA
utterances.text: On behalf of the accused Radic, it was already on the 1st of May that we raised an objection and we sent it in written form to Your Honours, to the Trial Chamber, and we adhere to that strictly because we would find ourselves in an extremely unfavourable situation, and this is our right; and in the name of honour and conscience, me, as Defence counsel who has been Defence counsel for 45 years, working in crimes of the highest degree, and in view of the fact that we are before a high institution, an eminent institution, that the world is looking up to and expecting decisions to be brought which shall form in the future judicial practice for all the lawyers of this world, in view of all this and in view of our professional ethics, we have to ask the Trial Chamber that we be provided, in order to be able to acquaint ourselves with it, the complete material, both in terms of the indictment of Mr. Radic, also the material which has to do with the indictment of Dr. Kovacevic, who has suddenly, I, as counsel, have to be in a position to be able to prepare myself to reply to the indictment, and it was very suddenly that we were informed about this joinder. So, Your Honours, in view of the fact that I neither have the complete material in regard of my -- of the accused that I'm defending and that we only have half of the file -- of course, we have been promised to get it -- and in terms of the material which charges Dr. Kovacevic, we have no knowledge whatsoever why he is being incriminated and what he is being charged with in respect of which my Defendant would be implicated, and we fail to see any link between that and the indictment of Dr. Kovacevic. That is why I wish to hear, on the basis of what argument and on the basis of what facts stemming from the material which was used in the process against Dr. Kovacevic, on the basis of what was the disposition arrived at that this should be linked with the trial of my Defendant, the accused that I'm defending. So, please, Your Honours, given my 73 years of age and my 45 years of experience as Defence counsel and also a member of the Amnesty International in London for 24 years and a champion of the abolition of the death sentence, I would like you to provide me with a satisfactory answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Guberina, we have, of course, received your motion, and we have considered it. We understand fully your position and, I should say, the position of other Defence counsel who have not received the material. Could you switch the microphone off, please? The position is that you have not had all the material; therefore, you say, naturally enough, that you are not in a position to respond to a motion about the conduct of the case until you have had all the material and the indictment, and that position we fully understand. Nonetheless, we have decided to list the matter today for this reason: that we want to hear argument upon it. In the case of Mr. Kovacevic, this is a matter which must be resolved quickly in order that his trial can begin, and this is an opportunity, the Trial Chamber feels, for these matters to be aired in public and for at least a preliminary view to be taken upon them. We have very much in mind the position which you mention. We have in mind your motion, and we shall not make any orders in respect of those accused who have not had the material until they have had it and counsel have had the opportunity to address us upon it. So that means this, that we will hear the matter. If it can be resolved by agreement, it will be. If it is rejected, it will be. If, on the other hand, we are minded to make orders which would concern your clients and upon which you wish to address us when you have had the material, then we will have that in mind and no orders will be made until such time as you have had the material. So at the moment, this is a preliminary hearing for us to at least understand what the motion is all about, and it may indicate a preliminary view or, if we can, make a final ruling. So you can rest assured we have your motion and your position in mind. With that, if I can turn next to the Prosecution. Ms. Hollis or Mr. Keegan, whoever is dealing with this more appropriately. This motion clearly raises important issues which have not been raised, I think I'm right in saying, before this Tribunal before. They concern the joinder of indictments and the concurrent hearing of evidence. And, of course, we have to have in mind that they must be decided against this background: On the one hand, the Trial Chamber is required by Article 20 of our Statute to secure a fair and expeditious trial for the accused. On the other, we must have regard to the protection of witnesses and victims. So, accordingly, we have to strike a balance of interests in deciding this matter. But let me, at the outset, say this, that in national jurisdictions, this is a matter, which it may be, can be sorted out between counsel, that it is a matter which is very much for discussion, the order of evidence, the way it is given, that sort of thing; and so if there is anything to be gained by discussion between counsel, time is available for it, and I would like to make that point as far as all counsel are concerned. We have this courtroom today and tomorrow and, indeed, for the rest of the week, it may be, so if there is anything to be done by way of agreement in order to resolve the problem, we, as a Trial Chamber, would encourage it. And perhaps, Mr. Keegan, I could begin by asking if there has been any discussion between counsel, discussion which you feel you can mention to the Trial Chamber -- of course, there is no need to mention something you don't want to -- but if there has been any discussion which you think might be of assistance to us, perhaps you would let us know. We notice, for instance, that Mr. D'Amato has made a suggestion about the way in which the case can be presented. It doesn't clearly follow your motion, but it is a possible compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There have not been any discussions with counsel on this issue, and with respect to Mr. D'Amato's suggestion, we don't feel that that addresses the central issue here, which is the protection for the witnesses and victims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I will hear you in a moment. The position is this, that we will certainly -- we will hear argument about it now. There will be the usual break, and it may be that time can usefully be spent during the break between counsel to discuss this matter, and if any round table discussion or anything of that sort could assist to resolve it, then you will have the time necessary. But before I hear you, Mr. Keegan, let me just make sure that I have got it right in my own mind what it is you are asking for because it seems that the Prosecution seek orders on three matters: First of all, you are asking for the case against all four accused be heard by the same Trial Chamber, and that, presumably, is under Rule 54, which gives us power to make such orders as may be necessary for the purposes of the conduct of the trial. Next, as I understand it, that in the case of the three most recently arrived accused, that is, Messrs. Radic, Kvocka, and Zigic, you are asking that the two indictments against them be tried together, and that will require a consideration of Rule 48 which allows persons accused of the same or different crimes committed in the same transaction to be jointly charged and tried. Thirdly, you are asking that the evidence against all four should be presented concurrently; and in that connection, there will be a need to consider Article 20 of the Statute which I have mentioned and Rule 75(A) which permits us to order appropriate measures for the protection of witnesses, provided that they are consistent with the rights of the accused. Presumably, the decision on the first two matters, that is, concerning the joint trial of all four and the joinder of the indictments, that the decision on those two matters really depends on our decision on the third matter, that is, in relation to the concurrent presentation of the evidence, because if we are against you on the third, the first matter falls and won't have to be considered in any event, and the second matter, that is, about the joinder of the indictments, that would be for the Trial Chamber who dealt with the trial of those three accused. Is that a right analysis of the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's right, except to the extent that with respect to your first point, strictly speaking, we are not requesting that they necessarily be heard by the same Trial Chamber. In a concurrent presentation of evidence, theoretically and technically it's possible to have two Chambers hearing the evidence concurrently. So that, as a technical matter, is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought that was what was in your motion, and I merely copied it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: But the first matter, Sir, was we decide as a matter of practicality to try to have all the accused assigned to the same Trial Chamber to facilitate that, but as a technical matter, if the decision was that concurrent presentation of evidence was appropriate but yet it was difficult to have the same Chamber hear all of the cases, it would be technically possible to have two Chambers hearing the same evidence. That's our only point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As a practical matter, I think you're probably correct, but I'm not so sure it's technically required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this before we go into the argument: Mr. Guberina suggested that some of the material had been served on Defence counsel in those three cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us as to how much and what your position is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I could. On the 5th of May, part of the supporting materials, that is, the statement of facts, the extracts of evidence relating to the individual accused, were hand-delivered by members of the OTP to the Defence team for Radic and Kvocka, and then on the 5th of May -- excuse me, the 7th of May, the supporting material, including statements related to the individual accused, were delivered to Mr. Tosic for the accused Zigic and the remainder of the statements to counsel for Kvocka. The remainder of the statements were also conveyed by courier to Belgrade to Mr. Guberina's office on the 7th of May. So from the OTP's perspective, we believe that all the supporting material has now been conveyed to all of the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I turn to defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what has been said by the Prosecution in respect of that, neither myself nor my defendant, Zoran Zigic, have received in our native tongue -- I left Banja Luka, actually material arrived the following day in the English language, so it was not of use to me. As regards the segment of my colleague, Guberina and I wholly subscribe to his opinion as regards the joinder in this particular case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Guberina, what have you received?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUBERINA
utterances.text: It is with particular pleasure, Your Honour, that I can say that on the 5th of May, when I was to see the Defendant for the first time, indeed we did receive at 15 to 9 on the 15th of May a part of the material, and I should like to thank our colleague, I believe her name is Ann, I should like to thank her very much, because when we asked her about the material the day before she told us, "Please, you will have to wait a bit" as she was taken a bit by surprise and as I myself was taken by surprise because that had been some twenty days after the indictment had been served on us without having received any supporting material then our colleague Ann asked where we were so that she could contact us that very evening by telephone and give us a part of the material on the next day. So that part of the material which we have received is this. That is it. We also said that for the purposes of the defence, please send it to us also in the English language; we will have it translated. And we did so. It is here. But we have no possibility -- we really cannot accept the fact that the Defendant has not received this because we want to go through it together with him once the complete material has been made available. We, of course, signed the receipt of that part of the material on the day that we received. Now, if anything has arrived in the meantime, and I can see that the OTP is referring to material dated the 7th of May, I cannot say at this particular point in time whether I can accept it because I am not sure whether it has indeed arrived. If it has, I will be most grateful and we will certainly acquaint ourselves with the substance of the material, but this will not detract from nor change our principal attitude, which is that we will ask the Trial Chamber that we be given a certain period of time, which we need in order to familiarise ourselves with the material in full and discuss it with the Defendants so as to be able to address this court and say that we do indeed appear as Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Grahovac, can you assist on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Concerning our client, Mr. Kvocka, our position remains that the proceedings for all the accused should be separate and our position is negative on the joinder of the proceedings for Messrs. Kovacevic and Zigic in question. And I think, Your Honour, that you have received our preliminary motion as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure we have. I don't know that we've received anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Dated the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm told it has been filed. It hasn't reached me. But can you help us? I should have asked you this before. Where is Mr. Simic? He is Defence counsel, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I am replacement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know you're standing in and we're very grateful to you for doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I think he was prevented to come, but next time, I think that he'll come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to make, if you can, make some inquiries as to where he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: During the day, and perhaps you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because he should be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might further clarify on this issue of the disclosure? At the initial appearance of Kvocka and Radic as well as at the initial appearance of Zigic, the temporary counsel assigned at that time, who were counsel appearing in other cases before the Tribunal, on the record, requested that they not receive, that they not be given the supporting materials, and that rather that the office of the Prosecutor wait until permanent counsel or counsel of choice were assigned and that they arrived at The Hague to see their clients and that they then be given the supporting material, and that is why the delay has been up until this point because we have been waiting to get full answers on assignment of counsel. Unfortunately, we received Mr. Guberina's request on the same day that he arrived here, which accounts for the surprise he attributed to Ms. Sutherland, because we only received the request itself and then he was here on the same day. But it's our understanding that I believe much of the material has been translated now into Serbo-Croatian, although not the statements themselves, but the other supporting material, the extracts and the other material. I will have to verify that, however. But as you know, the translation resources are a bit scarce, and it's our understanding that some, but not all, may have already been translated, and if so we will endeavour to provide that today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I think we may ask you to do, Mr. Keegan, is to find out, so we have a final updated position today sometime, as to what has been delivered and in what language and what, if anything, is outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We know that all of the material has been sent, Your Honour. Whether it passed counsel in transit, but it has all been sent in the English language, and the Serbo-Croatian language we have been awaiting, and it may at this stage be done or in part, and we will verify that before the close of business today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will hear your argument, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As Your Honour correctly pointed out in your summary of the issues and as we raised in our motion, the principal Article involved here is Article 20 of the Statute which sets out the objective for trials before this Tribunal, that is a fair -- that the accused be given a fair and expeditious trial. In conducting that trial, Article 20 points to two principles, and that is full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. By "protection," we submit, the Statute intends that term to encompass far more than physical security of the witnesses but also means their physical and mental well-being. The inclusion of the principle for the protection of victims and witnesses in Article 20, and in particular in Article 22, indicates the importance that must be given to the protection of victims and witnesses. The only limitation on the measures that may be taken by a Trial Chamber is where such steps may be in conflict with the rights of an accused to a fair trial. Article 22 of the Statute and Rule 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence further define the mandate of the Trial Chamber to order appropriate measures for the privacy and protection of witnesses. That mandate includes the method or manner in which testimony is given, and control of the questioning of the witnesses. In considering these issues, it must be noted that the principle of a fair trial does not equate to nor mean a perfect trial, nor does it mean a trial conducted in accordance with an accused's wishes or preferences; rather, it means a trial that accords the accused the rights set forth in Article 21 of the Statute. Provided those rights are accounted for in full equality, the other aspects of the trial process are within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, and in determining those trial processes, the Trial Chamber must give effect to the principles of Article 22 in Rule 75. As indicated in our motion, the joinder of the three accused, Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic, and the concurrent presentation of evidence against those three and the accused Kovacevic, is clearly warranted in light of the necessary protection for the victims and witnesses, for effective judicial economy and the interests of an expeditious trial for all of the accused. With respect to the topic of the protection of victims and witnesses. As described above, this issue concerns questions of both physical security as well as mental and physical well-being. The act of testifying, indeed the very determination to testify, and the necessary preparation that goes into that decision, are and can be traumatic events for all witnesses, for some severely so. To have to recount the horrors that these people witnessed or survived as direct victims is extremely difficult, as testified to by many of the witnesses in the Tadic case during cross-examination on the issue of media exposure. Many of the witnesses do everything they can to avoid having to think about the past, let alone be directly confronted by it, or to have to recount it in public. It is also true that there is not an unlimited supply of witnesses or victims that are willing to cooperate with or testify before this tribunal despite our best efforts and intentions, nor is it the case that the office of the Prosecutor has the ability to identify and locate all potential witnesses in a case. Accordingly, the witnesses who are identified and are willing to cooperate are indeed precious, and whatever efforts can be taken, consistent with the rights of the accused, must be taken. The impact of a lack of security for witnesses or even the perception of a lack of security can have significant consequences on the right of the international community to a fair trial. As has already been seen in other cases before this Tribunal, where security of information about witnesses has been breached for reasons totally unrelated to necessary investigation, witnesses have changed their minds and been unwilling to come forward and testify. We would, of course, point to the confidential annex which was submitted with our motion, Your Honour. Because the charges against all four of these accused flow from the same basic facts and events which occurred in the Prijedor municipality in 1992, the cases all involve the very same witnesses. This group of witnesses were utilised in the investigation process and their evidence was the basis for all three of the subject indictments. To require them to testify twice or possibly three times would pose a significant risk to their security and well-being, a risk which is neither justified nor required by a full respect for the rights of these accused. With respect to effective judicial economy, we believe this issue clearly speaks for itself. The limited availability of courtrooms at the Tribunal and the limited staff for all three organs of the Tribunal strongly argue for the conduct of one trial instead of two or three. Having to conduct two or possibly three trials that recount the exact same areas of evidence unnecessarily detract from the ability of the Office of the Prosecutor to conduct other investigations and trials, of the Trial Chambers to hear other cases which are already pending, and of the registry to be able to support both organs or to provide assistance to other Defence counsel and other accused. With respect to the issue of the right of an accused to an expeditious trial, it goes without saying that the principles and rights in Articles 20 and 21 apply to all accused equally. In a situation such as we have here present, we submit that the right of an expeditious trial is relative as to each accused and conditional on a determination of what would be the greater good; that is, what would best protect the interests and rights of the larger group of accused. A joinder and concurrent presentation of evidence would result in a fair and expeditious trial for all four accused. While it is true it might result in some amount of delay for the accused Kovacevic, the amount of which, of course, is unknown, given that we have no trial date at this present time, such a delay would not violate the standard of Article 21 of a trial without undue delay. Such a determination, with respect to a joinder and concurrent presentation, would be in accord with the precedents we have already considered in the Kovacevic case with respect to the issue of pre-trial detention, when we considered the standards under Article 14 of the ICCPR, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, as well as the European Convention on Human Rights. A further delay in this case, in order to effect a fair and expeditious trial for all four accused, would not violate the standard of "undue" delay, and we believe that is the key. The indictments related to all four accused establish themselves, the factual basis for this request for joinder and concurrent presentation of evidence. It is clear from a reading of the four corners of the indictments that the charges all flow from the very same events that were committed in the Prijedor municipality in 1992. Moreover, the accused Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic, are among the individuals subordinate to the accused Kovacevic, and their particular acts and crimes form part of the basis of his responsibility under Article 73 for the conduct of the camps. The joinder of Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic is in full accord with Rule 48 as referenced by Your Honour earlier. First off, they are charged with crimes in the same indictment related to the Omarska camp. And second, the joinder of the indictment which charges the accused Zigic with crimes in the Keraterm camp falls within the parameters of persons charged with different crimes committed in the course of the same transaction. That transaction being the ethnic cleansing of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population in Prijedor municipality in 1992. The joinder of the three, including the Keraterm indictment against Zigic, would also be in accord with the principles discussed above with respect to Article 14 of the ICCPR and Article 6 of the European convention and, of course, with the Articles 20 and 21 of this Tribunal Statute, and it is within the authority of the Trial Chamber under rule 54 to issue such orders as are necessary for the conduct of the trial. Further, as mentioned in our motion, the evidence regarding Keraterm would be relevant to establish the legal element of Article 5 charges that a widespread or systematic attack was committed against a civilian population in terms of considering the charges in the Omarska indictment against the accused Kvocka and Radic. And finally, as mentioned in our motion, all of the evidence with respect to those three accused, that is, Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic, all the evidence would be relevant for consideration against the accused Kovacevic on the charge of complicity and genocide and therefore forms the basis for the concurrent presentation of evidence request. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can, before you sit down, help us with this, Mr. Keegan: First of all, the word "transaction" in Rule 48 is defined in Rule 2 as "a number of acts or omissions, whether occurring as one event or a number of events, at the same or different locations, and being part of a common scheme, strategy or plan," and you would point, would you, to the ethnic cleansing as part of a common scheme, strategy or plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, as a shorthand term, you know, which has been commonly accepted for the events which occurred, it would translate -- if we want to put it in terms directly, to the last point I made about the Article 5 charges. There is a requirement for the Article 5 charges, of course, that the crimes were committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population. All of the acts which occurred in the Prijedor municipality in 1992 with respect to what's generally referred to as the ethnic cleansing, that is, the attacks on the villages or areas inhabited by Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats, the roundup of the population, the transportation to the camps, the crimes committed in the camps, as well as the unlawful transfer or deportation of the majority of the population, we argue, yes, is all part of that widespread or systematic attack, that being, if you will, a common plan or scheme, a transaction. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And turning to the practicalities, I think you said in your motion that there were 25 witnesses who you were proposing to call in the case of Dr. Kovacevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Those were the -- yes, sir, the 25 which we had firmly identified we intended to call in accord distance with your instructions. There will be additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just dealing with that aspect of it. And the 25, I think you also said in the motion, were also to be called in the case of the other three or the cases of the other three; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Sir. And with respect to some of those witnesses, they are, in fact, direct victims of the three accused, one or more of the three accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we have a position where there are 25 witnesses, at least, who are common to both trials?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But there are additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: They would also be common. As I indicated in my argument, Your Honour, the pool of witnesses which we have available to us were the witnesses who were -- formed the basis of the investigation and who almost all would be relevant -- would be called for both trials because it's the same pool which form the basis for the indictments, the individual indictments. There have, of course, been additional witnesses since '95, so I'm not going to stand here and say that all the witnesses we called were witnesses that were utilised in the -- in drafting those '95 indictments, but their development has been part of the continuing investigation and they would certainly be called to substantiate those indictments now, even though they weren't available to us at the time we drafted the indictments. But they will certainly be called now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just to give us some idea, in the case, first of all, Mr. Kovacevic, how many witnesses are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As we've indicated all along, Your Honour, it is our firm desire to limit the number of witnesses to 50 or less, and we intend to maintain that now, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And in the case of the other three or the cases of the other three accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It would be hard to -- if I could have just one moment, Your Honour? Your Honour, we, of course, would -- it's our intention to limit the number of witnesses to the amount necessary for the establishment of our case, and I am hesitant to give you a firm number at this time for any of the cases. Obviously, we're still pending the issue of the amended indictment in Kovacevic which would affect, presumably, could affect the number of witnesses, and with respect to the other three, since the preparation of those cases in the sense of for trial is still in its development, I'm hesitant to give you a firm number, but certainly not a large number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Turning to the practicalities of the situation, as I said earlier, the case of Milan Kovacevic was supposed to be heard today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But because there is an interlocutory appeal still outstanding, we have not been able to start. But I take it that you are ready for trial in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the case of the other three, what is your state of readiness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If the concurrent presentation were granted, Your Honour, we would be ready for those trials I think in fairly short order because, as I indicated, it would be the -- the core would be the exact same witnesses and what we would do now is look at what witnesses might be necessary to add onto this core group to facilitate all three indictments, that is, the two cases against the three accused and against Kovacevic. So I'm a bit hesitant, but I would certainly suggest, by July we could be prepared to proceed on all of the cases, as I believe we indicated in our motion that we thought we could be prepared by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well now, turning to the trials themselves, how do you foresee the trials being held? There won't necessarily have to be openings in all the cases, both cases or all the cases, because as I understand it, you are not asking for the joinder of the indictments against the three and also Mr. Kovacevic, you are asking for concurrent presentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you ever come across anything like that before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I myself have not personally participated in such a trial, but I am aware of them occurring and have been -- in offices I've been with have conducted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: They were drug distribution rings who overlapped, Your Honour, and so because there was a core group of -- again, a core group of witnesses against both groups involved in the drug distribution process and because of the witness protection issues, in fact, they simply brought all the accused together, conducted the presentation, that aspect of the evidence concurrently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These were trials by jury?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In both -- for those cases, they were judge alone trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And so what happened was this, was it, that the cases were opened separately, progressed in the normal way, but at the same time -- but then when it came to the common witnesses, the two cases were joined, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that case, much like this case, the vast majority of the evidence was common. The Prosecution would do a common opening, a joint opening, if you will, one opening address related to all the accused with respect to describing the evidence, and then proceed with the case. Now, certainly it is possible that the concurrent presentation could be limited to only those witnesses related to all of the accused. It's also possible, of course, to allow just the complete presentation of the evidence against all the accused from the Prosecution's side, the Court considering the evidence as necessary against the accused, and the Defence being involved only to the extent the evidence is relevant to their accused. At that point, once we proceed to the Defence case, as we indicated in our motion, it is possible, of course, at the request of the Defence and if the Chamber felt necessary, to allow separate presentation of Defence evidence. But we believe that the entire Prosecution case could be heard concurrently and, of course, it would be up to the Judges to determine which evidence was relevant to the particular accused because certainly there will be some evidence that may be relevant to the authority of the accused Kovacevic which is not necessarily relevant, although it might be in certain aspects, to the other accused. So we would argue that the full Prosecution case should be heard concurrently and allow the Judges to make the determinations of which evidence would be relevant to a particular accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That in effect would be a joinder of the indictment, at least for the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I even hate to qualify it, in practical terms as a joinder of the indictments because I don't believe it is. There are certain aspects of the evidence which would not be necessary and, of course, while all of the factual presentation is common to all the accused, certainly the qualification of that evidence in terms of the particular charges is not the same, and so it is not a complete joinder. And I would refrain from even, as a practical matter, trying to categorise it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The suggestion made by Mr. D'Amato, as you know, is that there should be a simultaneous hearing to this extent, that the cases would be heard side by side, one in the morning, one in the afternoon, as it were, so the witness would only be required or the relevant witnesses would only be required to come once, although they would have to give evidence twice. Now, while there may be practical difficulties about arranging that, it would secure, of course, that there were separate trials and that there were not a joinder in any way, and it therefore has that attraction. From what you have said earlier, I gather you oppose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The point of the bifurcated trial as it was referred to by defence, does nothing to address the concerns for the witnesses which are the central issues here that we are looking at and then considering in light of the rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial. The question from the Prosecution's perspective is, that if the concurrent presentation of the evidence is not itself violative of the accused's right to a fair trial, which we don't believe it is, then to that extent, once that determination is reached, in every measure which is necessary for the protection of the witnesses, that being not only their physical security, of course, but their physical and mental well-being, must be taken under Article 22 and Rule 75. The problem with the suggestion by the Defence is, it does nothing to address the concerns of having a witness having to go through full examination on two separate occasions, whether it's possibly in the same day or, more likely in many cases, on different days, even if they are subsequent days. It still involves the witnesses having to give their direct testimony twice, be subject to cross-examination twice, to questions from the judges twice. So it does nothing to address the difficulties, the mental difficulties that witnesses have and the traumatic experience that they go through, many of them, in having to give evidence. And I can also foresee, Your Honour -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I see that, of course they would have to give evidence twice and go through the evidence in chief twice. It wouldn't add to the cross-examination. They would have that in any event. They would have however many Defence counsel were going to cross-examine. But I see that they would have to give evidence in chief twice. But as against that, it would address some of the other concerns about the security of witnesses, their having to travel here on more than one occasion, the delays between the various hearings, all that I see as putting pressure on the witnesses and putting pressures on their security. That aspect of the case would be addressed, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Presumably, Your Honour. I would suggest, though, as I mentioned earlier in my argument, under Article 22 and Rule 75, of course, this Trial Chamber has the right to not only modify the conditions or the manner in which a witness gives testimony but also to control the questioning of the witnesses. We don't believe that it is necessarily the case that all Defence counsel would have to cross-examine a potential witness, nor perhaps would they even want to. So we don't think that that is necessarily the case. Certainly, if it's to the point where the questions are merely repetitive and bordering on the issue of harassment, then certainly the Trial Chamber would be able to tailor the scope of the cross-examination. I hesitate because I'm also very concerned about crossing over into the issue of testimony here, but I would suggest that the experience of this Tribunal clearly indicates that the trauma suffered by many of these witnesses after giving testimony might, in fact, prevent them from retaking the stand, particularly on the same day and even in subsequent days. I think the records and the experience in the trials to date speak for that. As to, I think, the experience of our cases here so far would also indicate that despite the best intentions of the Defence to continue with witnesses on the same day or perhaps next day, I think experience would indicate that probably would not happen often, particularly when you have transcripts which are readily available. You know, it's often the case where counsel would want to get the transcript of the witness's prior testimony before questioning them in the subsequent hearing on the matter. Whether that could happen in the same day or not, I don't know if it's possible. I think it would put a huge strain on the reporting system certainly, and then in that case might occasion delays of one or two -- certainly the more days that the witnesses stay in the Hague, the greater risk they are here being discovered and exposed, the longer they're away from home, the noticeable absence has the effect of affecting the potential security risk, many of them come from small towns or villages and it's readily apparent when they're gone for a long period of time. Whether they're coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina or other areas in the former Yugoslavia or even as refugees, given the status of refugees, any time they travel, it's a noticeable event. So we believe that, in fact, it doesn't necessarily address the security risks and concerns. And we do not believe that it would proceed as smoothly as the Defence suggests given our experience here to date, and we believe again the fundamental question is whether the current -- concurrent presentation of evidence would violate any of the requirements of Article 21 which are the requirements for the accused for a fair trial, and again, Your Honour, we believe the answer on that particular question is "No." So if the focus is Article 21 and the accused's rights, we do not need to discuss now deviations on what would be the maximum concerns for witness security and protection, that we focus on the rights of the accused and consider whether just concurrent presentation would violate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as any delay is concerned from counsel wanting to see the transcript of any testimony which was given in an earlier trial, that would seem to me to be totally unnecessary. If they wanted to, they could attend the hearing of the witness and take a note of it, and they could then cross-examine from that. So that side of it I don't see as a problem. The issue which is raised by the Defence, by Mr. D'Amato, is the potential prejudice which may be involved, and that's why I suggested this was, in effect, a joinder of the indictment. The potential prejudice which may occur from defendants having different interests to serve in the conduct of their defence. Of course, if you have a joint indictment, then there can be no argument about that; that is the way the trial is conducted. But if you have separate indictments and then try and present the evidence together, there is a risk, isn't there, that the Defence will sustain prejudice from the cross-examination which one or other Defence counsel may engage in, that they may have an interest which is completely contrary to the interest of the other Defence counsel, and the example, of course, was given in Mr. D'Amato's motion or response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but as we indicated in our reply, the trial process as a search for the truth is going to define the facts regardless of the interests of a particular accused. To the extent that the same witnesses are testifying and are giving the exact same evidence against the individual accused, whether it's in one trial or three, the same facts presumably are established and found by the Trial Chamber. So to the specific example of the armed conflict in Prijedor, whether the Defence for the accused Kovacevic would want to argue that an armed conflict establishes -- relates to a motive as to why there were attacks against the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population, that's an issue, as we indicated, that we don't think is a particularly viable option to begin with since the motive is irrelevant to the issue of the genocidal intent. So we think that the trial process, because in this the circumstances as we indicated, you have the same evidence being put forth to the Trial Chamber against all of these accused, it really matters not what particular legal strategies they may adopt in terms of arguing against the indictment against their accused. At the end of the day, the same amount or the same category, qualification or quality of evidence, is going to be adduced before this Trial Chamber. Certainly in the first trial. The problem is, from the Prosecution's perspective, having to conduct two or three trials may, in fact, deny the international community and the Office of the Prosecutor the opportunity to present a fair trial for the international community because we may not have those witnesses if we have to conduct two or three trials because they may not be willing to testify again. And that is the essential point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point is not an idle one, because if you have a joint indictment then, of course, the Defence can't complain if they use different strategies and damage one another. But if the indictment isn't joined, normally of course, the other Defence counsel aren't there, and the Defendant then, as it were, has a trial on his own, without suffering the risk of damage of cross-examination from another Defence counsel. This is the point that Mr. D'Amato makes. Now, as I say, if you have a joint indictment, then the problem doesn't arise at all, and no complaint can be made. But if the indictment isn't joined, in the normal course of events, the trials would be totally separate, and so a defendant would not have that disadvantage. Now, the procedure which you're suggesting of trying the cases together, would, it seems to me -- this is, of course, subject to argument -- but it seems to me to run the risk which Mr. D'Amato raises in his motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I -- what we believe is that if you were to follow the argument that if these were joined indictments, the joinder, the prejudice to the -- because the prejudice is still going to be there to the individual accused. They may want to argue different theories for the defence. So if you take that as the first premise, that the prejudice exists whether it's an official joinder or not, if you then say that if there was a technical joinder, the fact of the technical joinder would outweigh the potential prejudice to the accused such that the joint trial would occur, it is our position that then you really are only making the same determination for the concurrent presentation of evidence, you simply aren't using a technical legal determination, you're using the question of an analysis of the fundamental rights. And so we suggest that if you could find that if these indictments were technically joined, that would overcome the prejudice given the interests of witness security and protection and that the potential prejudice to the accused does not outweigh those interests as well as the other interests of judicial economy which we mentioned, then we believe you can find the same -- reach the same determination without that technical joinder by simply going through the same analysis, that it's the same basic evidence, the same pool of witnesses, the same documents, et cetera, would be presented for all of these cases to a large extent. That that evidence is going to lay before the Trial Chamber a certain set of facts which the Trial Chamber will then determine the guilt of the accused. That is not going to change whether it's a technical joinder or not. And the potential variations in Defence strategy won't change whether there's a technical joinder or not. So we believe that that technical joinder is not necessary to reach the appropriate determination that the concerns for witness protection and safety as well as the other concerns for judicial economy outweigh possible prejudice to the accused by virtue of potential arguments they'd want to make because we must, of course, remember that from the Defence side, this is all purely hypothetical at this point. They, of course, are not required to put on any evidence at all, nor advance any theory. They're not required to cross-examine any witnesses, if they don't wish to. So we do not know and cannot say for certain what their defences will be or they intend them to be at this time. And given that framework, in light of the known parameters of what the Prosecution must prove in its case with its evidence, we believe that the same determination can be reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Unless there is anything else you wanted to say ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. D'Amato, we will hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I begin just with a point of order? Mr. Keegan referred to a reply. We have not received any reply. Did he write a reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, if you have written a reply, this is the second time in two appearances here that I am getting it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. D'Amato, through the Bench, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we looked in our box this morning. There was no reply. I didn't get it by fax. And this is the second time that I'm getting it the instant I'm getting up to give an oral argument. It's a little unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you should have a copy. No doubt you would like some time to look at it. We can take the break rather early if it is more convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: I can proceed with my argument, and if there is anything that is left over by virtue of the reply, and if you give me a little more time later, I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to adjourn at half past eleven, so make a start, Mr. D'Amato.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to make a start without the benefit of the wonderful reply that awaits me. I would like to address Mr. Keegan's remarks starting from the end and working back to the beginning because I think those are the ones that are freshest on our minds. When he says it's all hypothetical at this stage, we don't know what the Defence will do, that's of course true, but Rule 82B says "in order to avoid a conflict of interest that might" -- "might cause serious prejudice to an accused," the word "might" is an invitation for us to look at this stage, pre-trial, to see whether these hypothetical situations could arise. So I don't think it's fair to say that just because we're talking about hypotheticals, that there's something wrong about that. We must talk about hypotheticals if we're trying to assess the probability of a conflict of interest that causes serious prejudice. With respect to Your Honour's point about a joint indictment would cause no problems, let me say this: Let's suppose, first, that Dr. Kovacevic was indicted for 15 counts of genocide and all the others that the Prosecution would like to add and his trial were all by itself. Well, of course, there would arise those prejudices that we're talking about. He would have to determine what his theory would be when it comes to genocide versus, say, crimes against humanity, and there would be a difficulty. But that difficulty would be under our control. The attorneys for the Defence would be able to make a strategic decision which way, which theory to go, given the fact that he's being charged with these incompatible crimes. But that's fair. What would be unfair would be to join our trial with other Defendants whose sole interest is incompatible with ours. So that when Your Honour made the suggestion that there would be no problem if there were a joint indictment, with all respect, if there were a joint indictment, I would have to move for a separation of trials given the incompatibility of genocide with crimes against humanity. The proof is entirely different, as I tried to point out in my brief. So that the problem is not solved by assuming that it's only a technicality that there be a joint indictment; as a matter of fact, if there were a joint indictment, we would have to move for separate trials and we'd be having the exact same argument we're having now; that is, are these two crimes compatible? Is it fair to pit one set of Defendants against another on factual issues, on basic factual issues of the trial? And I want to get to that in a minute, but I just wanted to make that point about the joint indictment, that it's not a technicality but it would result in the same problem. The point that was raised just before that with respect to my suggestion about a bifurcated trial, Mr. Keegan raised a number of issues of the trauma on witnesses who might have to speak twice in the same day, et cetera. That may be. There may be problems with that. I only made a suggestion. It's the Prosecution's motion here, and I only came back with a suggestion that, admittedly, is not 100 percent perfect, it can't solve every problem, but it is put forward in the spirit of trying to help with respect to the witnesses, as Your Honour pointed out. They still only have to make one trip here and not two. I think that Mr. Keegan is asking for a muddle. The trial that he envisages would be a disaster. There would be conflicting evidence throughout and Defence teams arguing against each other. This is evident from what he said in response to Your Honour's question about what a transaction is. It was very interesting when you asked him the definition of a transaction. His response was: It's all part of the Article 5 crimes. That's fine. But we're being charged with Article 4. The genocide is not -- he never mentioned the problem of genocide with respect to transactions. Our position is that Dr. Kovacevic is being accused of genocide; that's quite different from the ethnic cleansing that Mr. Keegan is talking about, or at least it could be quite different. Ethnic cleansing could be accomplished without destruction, in whole or in part, of a minority group. It could be accomplished, for example, by deportation, which is, as Mr. Keegan acknowledges, an Article 5 crime. But the transaction -- let's not get muddled with respect to what a transaction is, because once we are clear about that, it's pretty clear that it doesn't -- it's not something that would link our trial with that of the other Defendants. Mr. Keegan asserts that the linkage between Dr. Kovacevic and the other three Defendants has to do with the fact that they are subordinate to him, and therefore, the evidence of their crimes reflects back on Dr. Kovacevic. Your Honour, that's a bald assertion. There's not an iota of proof about that. There's nothing in the indictment that brings up the names of these other Defendants in connection with Dr. Kovacevic. It is just an assertion. If we disprove it at trial, then it would be incredibly prejudicial at the trial for us to be hearing all the evidence against the other three Defendants when we have shown that there isn't a link. It will still create a psychological barrier for the Court to see Dr. Kovacevic's case clearly. Now, if there were a link, then there might be something to the argument that has been made. But it is a sheer assertion. He doesn't establish a link by simply asserting it, and that's all he's done. And without that assertion, there's no link at all. My main point, though, after these preliminaries, is that let's assume Mr. Keegan's arguments are 100 percent persuasive with respect to the need for protecting witnesses, the need for this Tribunal to get on with its business, the limited funds at its disposal, the interests of justice. One hundred percent conceded. Nevertheless, we're facing here a textbook case of conflict that will cause serious prejudice. It is impossible to have a fair trial if situations arise where one Defence lawyer is trying to establish an evidentiary fact and the other Defence lawyer is trying to disprove that same fact. I'm not talking about culpability, I'm not talking about one Defence attorney saying, "Well, my client didn't do it," I'm talking about the basic fact. And the suggestion I gave in my brief -- which I know the other Defendants haven't heard yet -- suppose there is a Serb who is taken to one of these camps near Prijedor. In fact, Witness P might be an example of such a person, although he wasn't taken to the camp, but reading his statement, here is a Serb who is sympathetic, perhaps, with the other side. This Serb is taken to the concentration camp and interrogated. Why? Because they want to know whether he's loyal to the Serb cause or whether he's loyal to the opposition. That was one of the reasons to have a detention camp, is to sort people out. Let's assume that this Serb detainee dies in the prison, in the camp, and the defendants are accused of murder. They will, of course, try to argue that the Serb -- the victim was not killed by them nor by any other guard but perhaps died at the hands of his fellow prisoners. In other words, an alibi excuse that would suggest, "Yes, he died in the camp, but not at our hands, he died at the hands of his fellow prisoners who, for whatever reason, murdered him." That would be a fair alibi defence for them to assert. But what would Dr. Kovacevic want to argue? Strangely enough, because he's being accused of genocide, Dr. Kovacevic would want to argue that these Defendants, in fact, murdered this victim. They would argue the absolute opposite of what the other Defendants are arguing because Dr. Kovacevic wants to show that people were killed in the detention camps not because of their ethnicity or racial or national background because they were opponents of the Serb forces, and this Serb who was killed is proof that it was not a genocidal campaign at all but it was a civil war sorting-out kind of campaign. So we would have the crazy, the absolutely unjust situation at a trial where the Prosecution could sit back and smile and watch the Defendants tear each other apart. Two sets of lawyers arguing whether this person did it or didn't do it, whether the other person did or didn't, and it would be a farce, and I think that is an overwhelming textbook example of why there would be serious prejudice at a trial like this when you're trying to mix genocide in with crimes that are incompatible with it, that are evidentiarily incompatible; and therefore, no matter how much deference we give to the Prosecution's arguments about fairness to witnesses and everything, the Rule 82B is very clear: In order to avoid a conflict of interest that might cause serious prejudice to an accused, what could they have in mind that would be a better example of Article 82B than the case I just gave you that will inevitably come up in this trial, not just once but many, many times. Every time the other Defendants want to prove that there was no armed conflict, we would want to prove that there was. There would be a clash at every stage of the argument. We'd want to prove that there was armed conflict so that there was no overriding genocidal intent but, rather, was a civil war intent. They're going to want to prove that there was no armed conflict because they want to prove -- because they're being charged with war crimes and violations of the Geneva Convention. So all the way throughout the trial there would be an example of what Rule 82B is trying to avoid, and therefore I think that no matter -- it would be very good to try to solve the problems of the witness protection, but this way would ensure the unfairness of the trial to our client and, undoubtedly, to the other clients. Finally, one little word about expeditious trial. Even though Mr. Keegan is ready to proceed with a trial against everyone, the Defendants in the other cases would probably ask for 60 days to prepare. That's their right. And therefore, Dr. Kovacevic's trial would be postponed for two months more. He has been in jail a long time now, and it is his turn to come to trial and not to wait an additional two months for the trial to start. That's one reason I think the bifurcated motion makes a little sense. We could proceed with that without any of these joint witnesses, and maybe the happy conclusion would be that there would be no need to continue on with the trial if the Prosecution fails to prove that Dr. Kovacevic had the requisite intent to participate or to be complicitous in a genocidal plan. I see that I maybe just got under the wire, and with the possible reservation of possibly addressing anything that's in the reply brief that hasn't been covered, we rest our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be a break of 30 minutes now. Any remaining Defence counsel who would like to make any submissions, we will hear them then. Just one moment while I consider something with my colleagues. Mr. Keegan, we have just considered the position generally. We can't, clearly, make any binding ruling or anything like at the moment because we haven't heard your reply, we haven't heard all the arguments, and we need to do that. But it may be that you would like to consider further -- we have heard your position about it, I know -- but it may be you would like to consider further Mr. D'Amato's suggestion as a way of proceeding. We do have in mind the problems which the witnesses have before this Tribunal, we do have in mind our duty towards their protection and security, and clearly they are matters which have to be at the forefront of any consideration. But as I said at the outset, we have to balance that against the rights of the accused to a fair trial. Now, it would seem to me that it might be possible by agreement to reach some sort of compromise which would allow those interests to be properly balanced and also to secure as expeditious trials as we possibly can, given the shortage of time. For that reason, I am going to allow an adjournment of 40 minutes in the hope that during that time it may be possible for counsel to have a word together to see whether some agreement can be reached on these matters. If you would like more time, then send a message, and you will have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. But for the moment, ten past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 12.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato, have you had the opportunity of seeing the other submission by the Prosecution, the reply? Have you had the opportunity of seeing that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have. I perhaps would have changed the emphasis or tone of what I said, but I don't see anything to add at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it that useful discussions have taken place during the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Useful in the sense that we have realised the gap, the chasm that separates us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remaining Defence counsel, I know the position which you have adopted so far, and particularly what you say about not having received any or sufficient material. But if there is anything you want to say about these matters, I will hear you now. Yes, Mr. Guberina, is there anything you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUBERINA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we thank you for the possibility that you have given us, if need be, from the standpoint of the Defence, to say something. However, having heard the proceedings so far, I would like to say only that I do not wish to use my opportunity because I don't wish to disturb you and I remain by the motion that we submitted, and that would be it for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does anybody else want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the Defence of the accused Zoran Zigic, I agree with the stance of my colleagues as far as the procedure; however, as a long-term former prosecutor, I would have certain comments concerning the stand of the Prosecution about the motion for joinder. Taking into account the Prosecution and their aims, I feel that the reasons cited were not argumented [sic] for several reasons. As far as the stance of the Prosecution regarding the traumatic experience of the witnesses, we have a question that should there be a possibility for the witnesses in separate proceedings to come out with their testimony, we feel that this would be favourable to the Prosecution in view of the fact that the witnesses could remember all of the circumstances and all the questions that they are supposed to respond to. Furthermore, the claim cannot be accepted that these are the same witnesses because, looking at both the indictments, it is obvious that this is a detention centre, Keraterm and Omarska are two of them, and the incriminated acts, so our defendants are not the same for both camps so that we cannot talk about the fact that the same witnesses are therefore all of the accused. As far as the economy of the Prosecution in the name of truth and justice, we feel that the space and lack of personnel cannot be a reason for conducting one trial which, as far as the joinder of the indictments, the representative of the Prosecution has said that in order to have one trial and not to have a joinder of the indictment, I think that this would be a unique example in International Court because you cannot have one proceeding without joinder of the indictments. As far as the witnesses which would be heard in this one trial, there is a question of whether, in such a process, situation, we would be in the position to have the statements of the witnesses, in view of the stance of the Defence, could in some way be beneficial to the Prosecution in order to expand the indictment to other acts as well as to other persons. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as for the Defence of Mr. Kvocka, the opposition is negative. We are against the joinder of proceedings and cases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, is there anything you would like to say in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. With respect to the citation to Rule 82, as one of the reasons -- or the primary reason, standard, which the Defence asserts would require a determination against a concurrent presentation, Mr. D'Amato indicated that it's a determination that -- their interests that might cause serious prejudice. We, of course, would focus on the phrase "serious prejudice." And then, once again, in considering whether a concurrent presentation would violate the accused's right to a fair trial and in looking at Rule 82, in fact one can read that even if there was some prejudice, that is not a sufficient basis to deny the concurrent presentation of evidence but, rather, would have to rise to the level of serious prejudice against the accused because, again, the right to a fair trial applies to both parties, not just to the accused, and that the interests of the protection of the victims and witnesses, which is also a mandate for these Trial Chambers, does have an effect on that issue or the question of what is a fair trial and what kind of prejudice would be sufficient to negate the otherwise requirement to consider witness issues. Now, with respect to the issue of the transaction, and Mr. D'Amato referred to my analogy to Article 5, that was simply in terms of trying to put it in context of charges. Of course, the definition, as cited by Your Honour, quite clearly indicates it's not relegated directly to any particular charge or form of charge, nor is it related to any particular crime; rather, the argument of the related transaction here, as I indicated, is that the concurrent events in Prijedor during 1992 itself forms a transaction which I tried to then break down or categorise under the rubric of "ethnic cleansing," as it's commonly referred to, or made the analogy to the issue of a widespread or systematic attack which, of course, is an element under Article 5. But, in point of fact, it's not solely related to Article 5, and, of course, the same transaction of facts, which is the issue here in the concurrent presentation of evidence, that is, the presentation of facts, that same transaction of facts could be relevant to or is relevant to charges under Articles 2, 3, 4 and 5. Rule 48 supports that argument in that in its terminology where it discusses that individuals charged with same or different crimes in the course of the same transaction, obviously recognising that again the same facts can make one liable for more than one type of crime. With respect to the link of the other three accused, Kvocka, Radic, and Zigic to Kovacevic, Mr. D'Amato indicates that's a mere assertion. Well, in fact, when one reviews the indictments, the indictments themselves clearly indicate why they would fall within the personnel who were subordinate to the accused Kovacevic and therefore form part of the basis, their acts forming part of the basis for his responsibility under Article 7(3), and more particularly when one reads the supporting materials or statements that accompany the indictments and those three accused are prominently mentioned, it makes it very clear how they relate. Mr. D'Amato tries to chalk up the problem with respect to concurrent presentation of evidence to incompatible crimes. Well, the issue here is not the crimes, it's the facts which would be presented in that evidence, and the whole point of the motion is that the facts to be presented to this Trial Chamber would be the same for all of the accused. The application of those facts to the law may differ or vary as a result of the particular charges, but it's the basic underlying facts which are the issue here, and those facts will be the same. As we indicated in our response to the Defence motion for bifurcated trial which was filed on the 7th of May, we indicated that the main problem with the Defence suggestion is that the Defence suggestion is based on a fundamental misperception of the indictment against Kovacevic. The Defence, in paragraph 10 of their motion, asserts that the accused Kovacevic is not charged with participating in or even witnessing any of the alleged atrocities in the camps, instead the accused is charged with participating in an alleged plan that was intended to bring about the physical destruction of detainees in the camps on account of their membership in Muslim or Croat groups. That as far as Dr. Kovacevic is concerned, his alleged participation in the plan occurred, if at all, entirely outside the boundaries of the detention camps. They then posit in paragraph 11 that if the Prosecution fails to prove that the accused was criminally implicated in an alleged plan or conspiracy to commit genocide, then the accused would stand acquitted. These assertions are a gross misapprehension of the indictment against Kovacevic. In determining the scope of the charge, the indictment must be red in toto, and that indictment does not limit the accused's culpability or planning, nor is he, of course, charged with conspiracy and genocide. Further, while it's true that we would not have to prove the accused witnessed atrocities in the camps in order to prove his guilt, the indictment does not exclude the possibility of such evidence as relevant to prove his guilt. Finally, the Defence completely ignores the reality that the accused is charged both with individual criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1) and 7(3); and, of course, under 7(3) it would be the very acts committed in the camps by the accused such as Radic, Kvocka and Zigic that would form the basis for his liability for complicity. The relief requested by the Defence for Kovacevic ignores the relationship between the criminal conduct which is the subject of the indictments against the other three accused and the charge against this accused Kovacevic. The charge against Kovacevic indicates that between April '92 and January '93, Milan Kovacevic did, by his acts and omissions, commit the offence, and so therefore, it's that framework within which the other paragraphs of the indictment must be read, and it's clear then that from the language of the indictment, his responsibility for the crimes charged flows from the totality of his acts or omissions during that period, that is, 30 April of '92 until 31 December, '92. That would include, of course, any acts or omissions related to the conduct in the camps themselves, not simply acts prior to the establishment of the camps. I've already addressed the issue of the Defence's lack of appreciation of the individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(3) and what that would entail in terms of proof. As I raised earlier, the central point is that the concurrent presentation of evidence relates only to the Prosecution case, and the question here really is the presentation of the facts of the Prosecution case against all of the accused, and it is those facts which are common to all four and which can, by their common basis, form the proof of responsibility under all of the articles of the Statute. There is, of course, also the issue related to -- we must, of course, proceed under the current indictment, but obviously if the Appeals Chamber decides, for example, in favour of the Prosecution, certainly that would dramatically change the whole position of the Defence or the support for its argument of a bifurcated trial because then you would, in fact, have violation of the exact same articles for the accused, and one would wonder would the accused then ask to separate the charges in the indictment, of Kovacevic himself in that case, because of this alleged incompatibility? And we raise that point just to establish, in fact, that this argument of incompatibility is a purely hypothetical one and one which has no basis in actual presentation of facts within a courtroom for determination of individual responsibility for crimes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In ruling on this motion, we bear in mind, first, that we have a duty towards the protection and security of witnesses, but as I said at the outset, we also have a duty to secure a fair trial for all the accused. We have come to the conclusion that the course which is proposed in the motion is one which would be so prejudicial to the accused that a fair trial of all of them would not be possible. We also have in mind that, in the case of Dr. Kovacevic, an expeditious trial must be held, and were this motion to be allowed, it would hold up matters further. For those reasons, and for further reasons which will be given subsequently in writing, the motion put forward by the Prosecution is rejected to this extent: That the motion which calls for the case against all four accused to be heard together by the same Trial Chamber is rejected. The motion for the concurrent presentation of evidence against all four is also rejected. The motion which calls for the two indictments against Messrs. Zigic, Radic and Kvocka to be tried together is adjourned. It is a matter for the Trial Chamber which tries those Defendants to determine and not for us. The motion, if it is one, by the Defence, for what is being called a "bifurcated trial," is not a matter on which we shall rule. If the parties wish to consider the matter further, they can do so, and it can be re-presented, but at the moment, there will be no ruling upon it. For those reasons, as I say, this motion is rejected. That concludes the proceedings as far as the three more recently accused are concerned. This afternoon we shall proceed to hear a number of motions in the case of Milan Kovacevic. It may be of assistance to counsel in that case if we indicate the order in which we propose to hear those motions. We will begin by hearing the motion for the protection of victims and witnesses. We shall then deal with the motion in relation to the investigator. We shall deal next with the Defence motion concerning a code for the Prosecutor. We will then turn to deal with evidential matters and we will deal with the Prosecutor's request in relation to judicial notice and deal, finally, for the motion in relation to pre-trial admission. We will then have a status conference in closed session. Now, it may well be that we shall not be able to deal with all those matters this afternoon. We will continue tomorrow morning if that is the case. We shall adjourn for an hour and a half. I will say at ten past two.
